OSHA’s new guidance, “Opioid Overdose Rescue with Reversal Medications,” is part of the Great American Recovery Initiative, a government-wide effort by the Trump Administration prioritizing addiction treatment and recovery. The fact sheet provides practical information that focuses on empowering workplaces to recognize the signs of an overdose and act immediately.“President Trump has charged the Department of Labor with making recovery part of our workforce strategy, helping more individuals return to work and ensuring our businesses have the workers they need,” said Acting Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling. “Today’s guidance, released as part of President Trump’s Great American Recovery Initiative, is exactly the kind of action we were tasked with delivering on for the American people.”“President Trump has been fighting back against the deadly synthetic opioids infecting the entire illicit drug supply, from known illicit drugs to counterfeit tablets sold on the street or through fake online pharmacies,” said White House Drug Czar Sara Carter. “Because fentanyl has infiltrated the illicit drug landscape and acts as a chemical weapon against our people, it is critically important that the American workforce is familiar with drug overdose recognition and reversal. I am grateful to the Department of Labor for informing employers and workers about life-saving overdose reversal treatments like naloxone.”OSHA’s fact sheet highlights key opioid overdose preparedness strategies, including:Keep lifesaving FDA-approved reversal medications – such as naloxone or nalmefene – on hand. These safe, life-saving medications quickly restore normal breathing and generally have no effect if opioids are not present.Treat overdose kits like first aid by storing them in highly visible, easily accessible locations, just like automated external defibrillators or standard first-aid kits.Educate workers on how to identify critical symptoms of an overdose, such as slow or stopped breathing, blue lips or skin, pinpoint pupils, or unresponsiveness.Prepare for rapid action in an emergency by training workers to administer the medication, safely position the individual, and provide supportive care while waiting for first responders.OSHA’s guidance emphasizes that while these medications are critical, they do not replace emergency services. Workplace responders should always call 911 immediately because the medication’s effects are temporary and professional medical care is still required.The Department of Labor is committed to supporting workers’ safety and health on the job, along with partners at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, and other agencies.Read the Opioid Overdose Rescue with Reversal Medications fact sheet.Learn more about OSHA.

Attorney General Frey, along with the Attorneys General of 47 other states and territories, announce preliminary approval of their plan to distribute funds to consumers following multiple settlements with drug manufacturers accused of conspiring to inflate prices of generic drugs.

AUGUSTA – Attorney General Frey is urging consumers to check their eligibility for compensation for certain generic drug purchases and to submit a claim for compensation. This month, the U.S. District Court for the District of Connecticut granted preliminary approval of a plan, filed by Maine and a coalition of 47 other states and territories, to distribute settlement funds paid by generic drug manufacturers in exchange for settlement of claims that those companies illegally conspired to raise the prices of generic drugs.

The coalition previously announced settlements with the manufacturers Glenmark, Lannett, Bausch, Apotex, Heritage, and Heritage’s parent company, Emcure, totaling approximately $96.5 million. The multistate coalition’s distribution plan aims to return millions of dollars from those settlement funds to those potentially harmed by the elevated prices of the generic drugs that are the subjects of those settlements.

If you purchased a listed generic drug between May 2009 and December 2019, you may be eligible for compensation. To determine your eligibility, call 1-866-290-0182 (Toll-Free), email info@AGGenericDrugs.com or visit https://www.AGGenericDrugs.com. The deadline for submitting a claim is March 8, 2027.

Maine is part of a coalition of nearly all states and territories engaged in a series of antitrust cases, starting first in 2016. The first complaint included Heritage and 17 other corporate defendants, two individual defendants, and 15 generic drugs. The second complaint was filed in 2019 against Teva Pharmaceuticals and 21 of the nation’s largest generic drug manufacturers. The complaint names 16 individual senior executive defendants. The third complaint, to be tried first, focuses on 80 topical generic drugs that account for billions of dollars of sales in the United States and names 26 corporate defendants and 10 individual defendants. The States filed a fourth complaint earlier this year, alleging that Novartis AG, Sandoz Group AG and Sandoz AG, are liable for Sandoz’s alleged conduct and for fraudulently transferring assets. Seven pharmaceutical executives have been cooperating to support the States’ claims in these cases.

Maine Department of Labor announces October workplace safety and labor law training schedule

September 24, 2026

For Immediate Release: Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026

Media Contact: Autumn Mahoney, Communications Specialist media.dol@maine.gov

AUGUSTA - The Maine Department of Labor offers free workplace safety and labor law training to help employers, managers, supervisors, human resources professionals and others understand workplace safety requirements and Maine labor laws. The Department has announced its schedule of October classes, with trainings offered through SafetyWorks! and the Bureau of Labor Standards.

Registration is required, and space may be limited. View the October schedule and register for a class.

Unless otherwise noted, classes are held at the SafetyWorks! Training Institute at the Maine Department of Labor, 45 Commerce Drive in Augusta.

October Class Schedule

Fire Extinguisher/Emergency Action Plans/Workplace Violence Thursday, Oct. 1, 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m.
SafetyWorks! Training Institute, Augusta

Workplace emergencies include fire, medical, and workplace violence. This course covers the requirements of an emergency action plan, fire extinguisher use, and considering the potential for workplace violence. The SWTI Lab includes a fire extinguisher discharge activity to assist participants in learning how to use a fire extinguisher.

Bloodborne Pathogens Train-the-Trainer Friday, Oct. 2, 8:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. SafetyWorks! Training Institute, Augusta

This half-day class provides guidance on what is needed to be compliant with the bloodborne pathogen standard. This course will review written program requirements, training, documentation, Hepatitis B, and sharp logs.

Safety & Health Management Systems Tuesday, Oct. 6, 8:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. SafetyWorks! Training Institute, Augusta

Successful safety and health programs are more than just compliance with the OSHA standards. Injuries and illnesses are reduced when employers possess common elements to identify and address safety and health hazards. This course outlines roles and responsibilities, common principles, required functions and programs of a successful safety and health management system. This course prepares organizations who would like to pursue SHARP/ SHAPE.

Cold & Heat Illness Prevention Friday, Oct. 9, 8:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m.
SafetyWorks! Training Institute, Augusta

Whether your employees work outside or inside, cold and hot temperatures can be hazardous to their health. This class covers cold and heat temperature illnesses, signs and symptoms, and control measures to prevent and treat temperature related injuries.

Welding/Compressed Gas Tuesday, Oct. 13, 8:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m.
SafetyWorks! Training Institute, Augusta

This class covers the requirements of the welding standard, in addition to the storage and proper use of compressed gas. Proper inspection techniques of hoses, torches, and regulators will be demonstrated.

This course is designed for human resource or benefits professionals, accountants, business owners, managers, or payroll supervisors. Labor laws can be complex. ON APPLICATION FOR STAY [September 25, 2026] PER CURIAM. In 2022, the Missouri Legislature enacted a redistricting map for elections to the U. S. House of Representatives. In 2025, the Missouri Legislature enacted a new map. But under the Missouri Constitution as interpreted by the Supreme Court of Missouri, a new law such as the 2025 map does not take effect unless and until approved by voters in a referendum in the next election—at least where, as here, the number of voter signatures on the petition suffices to trigger a referendum. Therefore, on September 3, 2026, the Missouri Supreme Court ruled that the 2025 redistricting map “is not the law and has never been the law” in Missouri—and will not take effect unless and until approved by Missouri voters by referendum in the 2026 election. von Glahn v. Hoskins, ___ S. W. 3d ___, ___–___, n. 8 (Mo. 2026), App. to Emergency Motion 53–54a, n. 8. In short, as a matter of state law, the 2022 map—not the 2025 map—must be used in the 2026 congressional election. In the wake of that recent Missouri Supreme Court decision, a group of voters and candidates (collectively, plaintiffs) sued in federal cou rt. They contended that the U. S. Constitution requires Missouri to use the 2025 map in the 2026 election—even though the 2025 map cannot take effect under Missouri law unless and until it is approved by Missouri voters in the 2026 election.

As fall arrives in Maine, respiratory viruses such as influenza (flu), COVID-19, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), also return and begin to spread more widely as people spend more time together, indoors. The Maine Department of Health and Human Services’ Center for Disease Control and Prevention (Maine CDC) reminds Maine people and visitors to take steps to keep themselves, their loved ones, and neighbors healthy this respiratory virus season.

Respiratory viruses can cause fever, cough, sore throat, runny or stuffy nose, muscle aches, and fatigue. Some people are more likely to get very sick and need medical attention. These viruses can spread when an infected person coughs or sneezes. They can also spread from touching the surface with the virus on it and then touching your nose or mouth before washing your hands.

The Maine CDC recommends the following measures to protect yourself and others:

  • Stay home when you are sick.
  • Wash your hands frequently with soap and water.
  • Clean and disinfect surfaces and objects that people touch often.
  • If you are sick, consider wearing a mask around others.
  • Cover coughs and sneezes with a tissue or your elbow.
  • Avoid close contact with people who are sick.
  • Get vaccinated, as appropriate for flu, COVID-19, and RSV.

Vaccination is the most effective way to prevent respiratory viruses. Vaccines can also help make illness less severe and help prevent missed work or school. Getting a flu vaccine every year and staying up to date with COVID-19 and RSV vaccinations, if eligible, can help lower the risk of getting sick.

Consistent with the recommendations of the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Physicians, and American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, the Maine CDC recommends the following respiratory virus immunization for the 2026-2027 season:

  • Flu: Everyone 6 months and older should receive an annual flu vaccine.
  • COVID-19: Vaccination is recommended for
    • all children ages 6 through 23 months;
    • children and adolescents ages 2 through 18 years who are at increased risk for severe COVID-19 or who want to be vaccinated;
    • adults age 19 and older;
    • pregnant individuals.
  • RSV: Immunization is recommended for certain infants, pregnant people, and older adults.
    • Infants: RSV immunization is recommended for those younger than 8 months born during or entering their first RSV season, if they are not protected by maternal RSV vaccination.
      • Certain children ages 8-19 months who are at increased risk for severe RSV may also be recommended to receive RSV immunization during their second season.
    • Pregnant people: RSV vaccination is recommended during weeks 32 through 36 of pregnancy.
    • Older adults: All adults age 75 and older and adults 50-74 at increased risk for severe RSV illness.

To find the nearest location to get a vaccine, contact your local pharmacy or health care provider.

The Secretary of Labor and United States Trade Representative co-chair the Interagency Labor Committee for Monitoring and Enforcement (ILC). On August 26, 2026, the ILC received an RRM petition from the Liga Sindical Obrera Mexicana (LSOM), a Mexican labor union, and the International Lawyers Assisting Workers Network (ILAW). The petition alleges that Yokohama is violating workers’ rights to freedom of association and collective bargaining by retaliating against workers for engaging in union activity. The ILC reviews RRM petitions that it receives, and the accompanying information, within 30 days. After conducting this review, the ILC determined that there is sufficient, credible evidence of a denial of rights enabling the good faith invocation of enforcement mechanisms. As a result, the United States Trade Representative has submitted a request to Mexico that Mexico review whether workers at Yokohama are being denied the right to freedom of association and collective bargaining. Mexico has 10 days to agree to conduct a review and, if it agrees, 45 days from today to complete the review. Voters urged to look for .gov websites for official, trusted voter information 

AUGUSTA, MAINE – Secretary of State Shenna Bellows today warned Mainers to be vigilant when viewing voting information online. This included raising awareness of private sites that may give the false impression – by name, URL, and/or design – that it is an official election website. 

“It is becoming increasingly difficult to distinguish what is real and what isn’t online,” said Secretary Bellows. “AI and other automated tools help partisan operatives or cybercriminals create websites that look official even when they’re not. While some non-governmental sites about voting present accurate information, many do not.”

Many sites are designed to encourage citizens to register to vote and may in fact redirect visitors to official sites. However, many sites may require visitors to enter their personal information before they are redirected. Official state addresses will include .gov. For example, Mainers can register to vote at https://www.maine.gov/vote or find official election information by visiting the Secretary of State’s website at https://www.maine.gov/sos. 

“If you don’t see .gov in the web address, it is not an official state government website,” Secretary Bellows said. “If you are being asked to enter personal information like name and email address before you get to an official .gov link, then someone else is getting your private data. Instead of giving out private information to sites that might try to scam you or steal your data, go straight to the source at maine.gov/vote.”  

Secretary Bellows also encouraged voters to be careful when viewing election information on social media and always research and vet the information that they read. 

“There is unfortunately so much misinformation and disinformation out there, it can be overwhelming and difficult to know what’s true and what’s not,” said Secretary Bellows. “Everyone can play a part in reducing anxiety about the upcoming election by going to official sources and not sharing or posting unvetted and potentially false content. We have had safe, free, and secure elections in Maine for over 200 years, and we expect the same this November.”

Hello, this is Governor Janet Mills, and thank you for listening.

Well, last week I was privileged to witness a group of multinational soldiers complete a joint military exercise known as the Common Challenge 2026. Up in the mountains of Montenegro, among the chatter of many nations, I listened to dignitaries and servicemembers comment on the success of the day, on the readiness for the mission, and on the grit and pride of that international team.

My thoughts turned to Shakespeare, a bard of some four centuries ago, who could not have envisioned the future circumstances which we find ourselves in today, but who said prophetically and for all time: "the Readiness is all."

Readiness indeed. Readiness is what I saw in Montenegro last week. Readiness for things known and unknown, unexpected and expected.

I traveled there with Major General Diane Dunn and Maine National Guardsmen to Montenegro to observe that joint training mission and to meet with Montenegrin officials, military members, and citizens to celebrate the 20th anniversary of Maine's strategic partnership with Montenegro. I am the second governor to have visited Montenegro and celebrate this partnership.

In 2006, Maine and Montenegro formed that partnership to share training and military expertise, as Montenegro became a member of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, or NATO. Both the state of Maine and the people of Montenegro have benefited through this shared knowledge, through team exercises, and through progress in this strategic partnership.

Over the past 20 years, our servicemembers and Montenegrins have trained side-by-side, shoulder-to-shoulder, learning how to navigate challenging mountain terrain, practicing difficult search and rescue missions, confronting dangerously cold weather conditions, and defending the security of our respective regions. Montenegrin soldiers have traveled to Maine for engineering projects, and Maine National Guardsmen have traveled to Montenegro to respond to cyber-attacks on that country. 

While in Montenegro, Major General Dunn and I met with the Prime Minister and the President, Defense Minister, and Foreign Minister of the country to discuss the future of our relationship and the prospects for more collaboration. Collaboration in forestry research, in deep port uses, in trade, and in educational exchanges for the benefit of both regions.

Maine, like Montenegro, for instance, has a deep ocean port, which is an important gateway for trade. We are tackling threats of cybersecurity and threats from severe weather caused by climate change, just as they are. We too have a thriving forest products industry that is at the heart of our economy.

So I emphasized to the Montenegrins that Maine offers world-leading universities, community colleges, and private higher eds, who are all ready to work with Montenegro students to train the next generation of best and brightest leaders—broadening research and bolstering our mutual security.

I am proud of our own Guard members and of their determination to reach outside their own boundaries and zones of operation and zones of comfort to assist the people of Montenegro in addressing cybersecurity threats, in training and in military preparedness, and in maximizing the potential for international collaboration and expertise.

To properly commemorate the 20th anniversary of this bilateral commitment of the Maine National Guard and the Armed Forces of Montenegro, I've officially proclaimed September 17th as Montenegro-Maine Partnership Day, reaffirming our friendship with the leaders, the people, and the Armed Forces of Montenegro.

Maine and Montenegro have contributed our human and physical resources to this effort, and our culture, our character, and our courage have combined for the common good of humanity and for the common peace of our nations.

Maine and Montenegro are ready.

This is Governor Janet Mills, and I thank you for listening.

WHEREAS, Maine's relationship with the ocean has always been dynamic, shaped by changing communities, resources, markets, and conditions; and


WHEREAS, from the earliest Indigenous traditions of fishing, harvesting, and boatbuilding, to the shipyards that continue to connect Maine to the world, our people have long adapted to changing circumstances and found new ways to work on and with the sea; and
 

WHEREAS, many of the practices we recognize today as Maine traditions were once innovations themselves, developed by generations of Maine people who embraced new techniques, technologies, and ideas to pursue new opportunities while respecting the natural limits of the Gulf of Maine; and
 

WHEREAS, Maine's fishermen, sea farmers, boatbuilders, engineers, entrepreneurs, scientists, researchers, and inventors continue this tradition of ingenuity, mastering traditional craftsmanship, innovating new marine technologies and practices, and advancing ocean science, climate adaptation, and blue biotechnology; and
 

WHEREAS, as the Gulf of Maine experiences rapid change, the tenacity, expertise, and spirit of innovation that have long defined Maine's working waterfronts are more important than ever as we adapt to new conditions and pursue new opportunities; and
 

WHEREAS, the future of Maine's blue economy depends on continued investment in the people, research, businesses, and working waterfronts that have always transformed necessity into innovation, and innovation into the Maine we know today;
 

NOW, THEREFORE, be it resolved that I, Janet T. Mills, Governor of the State of Maine, do hereby proclaim the week of September 28-October 2, 2026 as
 

Maine Blue Economy Week 
 

and I encourage all Maine people to recognize and celebrate the ingenuity, expertise, and entrepreneurial spirit that has sustained our connection to the ocean and will help shape the future of Maine's blue economy.

In testimony whereof, I have caused

the Great Seal of the State to be

hereunto affixed GIVEN under my

hand at Augusta this twenty second day of

Attention Trading Partners: MIHMS Upgrade October Payment Cycle Changes and System Access Limitations

Sep 28, 2026

As previously communicated, the Office of MaineCare Services (OMS) is preparing to launch an upgraded version of MIHMS, MaineCare’s claims processing system. The upgrade is currently scheduled to go live on October 10, 2026. To support a smooth transition, OMS must implement temporary system access limitations and adjustments to payment cycles in October.  

From Friday, October 2 at 8:00 PM until Monday, October 12 at 8:00 AM, MIHMS will be in a “data freeze” while OMS completes final system readiness and transition activities. 

Please note that we have updated the FAQ previously shared, as of September 21, 2026. 

Changes to October payment cycles: 

Review this information and plan billing accordingly to prepare for the transition.

*As always, timely submission does not guarantee that the claim will process in time for the next payment cycle. OMS may take up to 30 days to process and pay a claim, depending on any edits or issues that may cause the claim to pend for manual review, as well as other processing requirements that may require the full 30-day timeframe. 

Preparing for the changes to October payment cycles: 

The HealthPAS Online Portal has returned to its previous regular operating hours. Providers again have 24/7 access to the portal, for additional flexibility and time to submit claims outside of standard business hours.   

We strongly encourage providers to submit claims approaching timely filing limits in the next few weeks to avoid potential submission delays. The planned data freeze does not modify existing Medicaid timely filing requirements. Providers remain responsible for ensuring claims are submitted within the established timely filing guidelines. 

Other system access limitations: 

Providers can find other expected impacts of the data freeze in this FAQ. We have updated the FAQ as of September 21, 2026. Topics include: 

  • HealthPAS Online Portal, including impacts on submitting claims, submitting prior authorizations, and checking member eligibility 
  • Provider Enrollment Application (PEA) 
  • Value-Based Purchasing Management System (VMS) Portal 
  • Paper & fax document submissions 
  • Provider Services & Member Services call centers 
  • Value Added Network (VAN) Trading Partners 
  • Prior authorizations for prescriptions and behavioral health services 
  • Electronic Visit Verification (EVV) 
  • Secure File Transfer Protocol (SFTP) 

You can also check the OMS Provider Resources webpage, in the first box of information called “Health PAS Online Portal,” for the most recent information about the upgrade.  

For questions or clarifications, please contact Provider Services at 1-866-690-5585. Please note, Provider Services does not have additional information beyond what is shared in this message and in the FAQ linked above.

Attention Trading Partners: Refresher Training for New MaineCare Partner Portal

As a reminder, the new MaineCare Partner Portal is scheduled to go live on October 12, 2026, at 8:00 AM. The new portal will replace the current HealthPAS Online Portal and provide enhanced functionality to support Trading Partner operations. We are adding additional live, virtual instructor-led training sessions to help Trading Partners prepare for the transition. 

As a reminder, recorded training sessions, training materials, user guides, Q&A documents from training sessions, and supporting resources are available through the MMIS Learning Center and will continue to be available after go-live. 

Please share this training information with staff responsible for claims, authorizations, referrals, account maintenance, and portal administration activities. Staff should not wait for refresher training to become familiar with the materials. 

Key Reminders

  • Trading Partner Administrator (R7) accounts will be migrated to the new portal. 
  • Additional users will be invited and managed by Trading Partner Administrators after go-live. 
  • Trading Partner Administrators (R7 users) should prepare for portal access and account setup activities by reviewing the training materials available in the MMIS Learning Center before go-live.

MMIS Learning Center Access and Course Registration Instructions 

Use the following steps to register for MaineCare Partner Portal refresher training.

    • If you need a new account, enter the enrollment key: De8pO9CBYXYB-aOCY8qp.

  3. From the Learner Dashboard, search for "TPT Refresher” using the Course Catalog or Search bar at the top of the window.  
  4. Click Choose Session and enroll in the session that best fits your schedule.

Supreme Judicial Court to Hold Oral Arguments at Three Maine High Schools

Date: 9/29/2026

The Supreme Judicial Court will hold court and hear a total of nine cases at three Maine high schools next week.

On Tuesday, October 6, beginning at 9:00 a.m., the Court will visit Katahdin Middle/High School in Stacyville to hear arguments in three appellate cases. Senator Trey Stewart extended the invitation to the Law Court. The three cases are scheduled to begin at 9:00 a.m., 10:00 a.m., and 11:00 a.m.

The Court will hear three appeals at Morse High School in Bath on Wednesday, October 7 at the invitation of Senator Denise Tepler. The Court will follow the same schedule with the first oral argument starting at 9:00 a.m., the second at 10:00 a.m., and the third at 11:00 a.m.

And on Thursday, October 8, the Court will hear three cases at Kennebunk High School at the invitation of Representative Daniel Sayre. Again, the schedule indicates that the first case starts at 9:00 a.m.

Students receive copies of the briefs in advance and, after each argument, the lawyers stay to answer questions from interested students. When the cases are decided, the schools receive a link to the decisions to share with the students.

Beginning in 2005, the Court has held oral arguments in actual appellate cases at over 40 Maine high schools around the state. In each school, the gymnasium, cafeteria, or auditorium is turned into a courtroom for the morning so that the students can observe the appellate process. The Court has visited schools from York County to Aroostook County; from Oxford County to Washington County; and many places in between.

Chief Justice Valerie Stanfill said, "We hope that providing real-time exposure to the third branch of government supplements the students' civics education and exposes Maine learners to the concept of justice. The practice of appellate law is rarely seen on television or in the movies. Creating a courtroom environment in a high school takes great effort on the part of the school administration and staff and we appreciate their extensive efforts."

The press is welcome to attend. The case schedule has been posted on the Courts website here.

Live video streaming of these cases, and all other Supreme Judicial Court oral arguments, is available here.

Photographs and video of students are subject to the rules of the high school, and the press is requested to contact school officials directly.

item.content:encoded: WASHINGTON – The United States and Mexico today announced the successful resolution of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) facility-specific Rapid Response Labor Mechanism (RRM) matter regarding theAkwel Juárez México, S.A. de C.V. (Akwel or the company) facility located in Ciudad Juárez, Chihuahua, Mexico. The United States and Mexico agreed on a course of remediation to address labor violations occurring at the facility, including employer interference in union activity and retaliatory dismissals of workers. That plan has now been implemented, and the denial of rights concerns raised in our request for review have been remediated. As a result, the United States Trade Representative has directed the Secretary of the Treasury to resume liquidation of unliquidated entries of goods from the facility.The measure marks genuine progress in safeguarding U.S. workers' ability to compete internationally, requiring Mexican producers to follow Mexican law and the terms of the USMCA. Actions taken during the course of remediation allowed the Akwel workers to elect a representative union and negotiate a collective bargaining agreement with improvements to wages and working conditions at the facility. This case represents another victory for the Trump Administration, whose America First policy prioritizes American workers by preventing foreign auto parts manufacturers from weakening worker protections to obtain an unfair trade advantage.The Department of Labor’s Bureau of International Labor Affairs and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative facilitated a resolution with the Government of Mexico (Mexico) to remediate workers’ claims at Akwel.Actions taken by the facility to address the matter include:Reinstating three workers with full backpay and benefits and paying full severance to six workers, based on their respective preferences; Restructuring human resources and labor relations management, and taking appropriate disciplinary action against staff who violated workers’ freedom of association and collective bargaining rights;Implementing and training all company personnel on its neutrality statement and guidelines related to freedom of association and collective bargaining, including a zero-tolerance policy for violations, and committing to retraining annually; Informing workers about the denial of rights at the facility by conducting meetings and posting notices at the facility to acknowledge Akwel’s unlawful and interfering practices and affirm the company’s intention to respect workers’ rights in the future;Installing and publicizing a complaint mechanism through which workers can report violations of their rights and breaches of company policies anonymously and confidentially; andMaintaining on the company website and in any internal communications platform the neutrality statement and guidelines, collective bargaining agreement, training materials, and information about complaint mechanisms maintained by the company and Mexico, such that the information is easily accessible to workers.Actions taken by Mexico to address the matter include:Monitoring the facility with regard to the obligations of the course of remediation and compliance with Mexican laws related to freedom of association and collective bargaining; Conducting in-person training that is structured to ensure all workers understand their right to freedom of association and collective bargaining and how to exercise it, including by informing workers of the denial of rights at the facility and educating workers on the conciliation process available to any dismissed worker;Conducting separate workers’ rights training for supervisors, human resources and labor relations personnel, and other high-level and “trusted” officials; Maintaining a direct email address, reporting platform, and telephone line for workers to anonymously report any potential acts of unlawful interference or other violations of freedom of association and collective bargaining rights, and timely investigate any allegations; and Imposing sanctions in accordance with Mexican law, including financial penalties, on Akwel for violating Mexican laws related to freedom of association and collective bargaining.BackgroundThe Secretary of Labor and the United States Trade Representative co-chair the Interagency Labor Committee for Monitoring and Enforcement (ILC). On October 24, 2024, the ILC received an RRM petition from Sindicato Nacional de Trabajadores y Empleados Especializados, Conexos y Similares de la República Mexicana (SINATAM), a Mexican labor union, along with ten workers as signatories. The petition alleged Akwel had violated workers’ right to collective bargaining and freedom of association by refusing to negotiate a collective bargaining agreement with the petitioner union, dismissing workers based on their union affiliation, and threatening and harassing workers to disincentivize their union activity. The ILC reviews RRM petitions that it receives, and the accompanying information, within 30 days. The ILC determined that there was sufficient, credible evidence of a denial of rights enabling the good faith invocation of enforcement mechanisms. As a result, on November 22, 2024, the United States submitted a request that Mexico review the matter. Mexico agreed to conduct a review and, on January 6, 2025, concluded a denial of the rights had occurred at the facility. Subsequently, the United States and Mexico agreed on a course of remediation. The end date of the course of remediation was January 31, 2026. The United States closely monitored compliance with the course of remediation.Read the full course of remediation.Read an unofficial courtesy Spanish translation of the full course of remediation.Read the letter to the Secretary of the Treasury.Learn more about the department’s work to make global competition fair for American workers.

item.title: US Labor Department obtains court order naming independent fiduciary for 401(k) plan of defunct WA-based aerospace company — U.S. Department of Labor — News Releases
item.description: SEATTLE – The U.S. Department of Labor has secured a court order to appoint an independent fiduciary to manage the abandoned 401(k) plan of a defunct Arlington-based aerospace company.The order, entered in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington, appoints AMI Benefit Plan Administrators Inc. as the independent fiduciary for the Commercial Aircraft Interiors LLC 401(k) Plan, which has been frozen since the employer shut down operations in 2023. In this role, the independent fiduciary will be able to distribute its assets to eligible former employees who have not been able to access their retirement savings because the only responsive company representative, Charles Pratt, lacked the legal authority needed to approve distributions. The independent fiduciary will also be able to formally terminate the plan.“The appointment of an independent fiduciary will give the participants in the Commercial Aircraft Interiors plan access to the funds that rightly belong to them,” said Liam Roberts, district director for the department’s Employee Benefits Security Administration in Seattle. “We urge all workers to contact the department for assistance when their retirement plan has been abandoned and they have not received the benefits to which they are entitled.”Under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act, all employee benefit plans are required to be managed by named fiduciaries. Without one, participants and beneficiaries cannot get information about their accounts or collect retirement benefits. The Commercial Aircraft Interiors plan has approximately $260,000 in assets and 59 participants.EBSA ensures the security of retirement, health, and other job-based benefits for American workers and their families. The agency is responsible for protecting more than 155 million workers, retirees, and their families, who are covered by approximately 2.8 million health plans, 837,000 private retirement plans, and 521,000 additional welfare benefit plans. WHEREAS, October 2026 marks the 81st anniversary of National Disability Employment Awareness Month; and

WHEREAS, workplaces across our state that are welcoming of the talents of all people, including people with disabilities, are critical to healthy communities and a strong economy; and

WHEREAS, while the employment rate of people with disabilities ages 16 to 64 in Maine has increased to 44 percent, it remains significantly lower than the 83 percent employment rate for Maine people without disabilities; and

WHEREAS, it is important that the State of Maine prepare all youth, including those with disabilities, for meaningful careers and an adulthood that includes employment; and

WHEREAS, Maine is an Employment First state, affirming employment as the first and preferred option for people with disabilities who receive services from state agencies; and

WHEREAS, people with disabilities, including people who are Deaf, Hard of Hearing, Late Deafened, Blind or with Low Vision make significant contributions to Maine's economy and communities; and

WHEREAS, activities during this month will reinforce the value and talent people with disabilities add to our workplaces and communities and affirm Maine's commitment to increasing access to good jobs and competitive, integrated employment for all workers, including those with disabilities;

NOW, THEREFORE, be it resolved that I, Janet T. Mills, Governor of the State of Maine, do hereby proclaim October 2026 as 

Disability Employment Awareness Month

throughout the State of Maine, and I call upon employers, schools, higher education institutions and other community organizations in Maine to observe October with appropriate programs and activities that celebrate the contributions of people with disabilities and promote access to good, in-demand jobs and career pathways such as registered apprenticeships for all Maine people.

Maine Forest Service report highlights effectiveness of forestry practices that protect water quality

October 1, 2026

AUGUSTA, Maine, October 1, 2026 - A new Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry Maine Forest Service (MFS) report underscores the effectiveness of environmentally friendly practices during timber harvesting. Released Oct. 1, the "Maine Forestry Best Management Practices Use and Effectiveness Data Summary" draws on hundreds of observations at timber harvesting sites across Maine.

This MFS study shows how forestry and timber industry professionals use recommended practices statewide. It also demonstrates that the risk to waterbodies greatly increases when they are improperly applied.

These measures, called Best Management Practices (BMP), are voluntarily implemented by professionals to help protect water quality in Maine's streams, rivers, lakes, and wetlands. They cover planning and application recommendations for activities such as stream crossings, road construction, and controlling erosion and sediment, the primary pollutants associated with timber harvesting.

Maines forest industry has made great strides in protecting water resources in recent decades, said State Forester and MFS Director Patty Cormier. The improvements weve identified through our BMP monitoring program are a testament to the ongoing value of the training that loggers, foresters, and woodland owners have participated in and applied. We thank them, our training partners, and collaborators for their contributions to this progress.

The report, released every two years, is the result of this monitoring from 2024 to 2025. It includes data from 165 timber harvesting sites and observations on over 700 individual activities, including around stream crossings, contaminants, and log landing placement.

This year's key findings include:

  • 74% of study sites applied appropriate practices on stream crossings. In many cases, they included planning to avoid crossings altogether. MFS emphasizes avoiding stream crossings when possible because they present the highest risk for sedimentation.
  • Soil movement monitoring found that, in 85% of cases, no sediment entered a water body. Of the 15% instances where sediment was recorded, 9% were in measurable amounts (~1 cubic foot or more of sediment), and 6% were trace amounts.
  • 87% of sites showed no evidence of chemical spills, a 10% decrease from the previous report. Reported spills ranged from minor drips to less than 10 square feet.
  • Progress on improving fish passage continues. Although the number of stream-crossing structures adequately spanning stream channels on haul roads decreased by 5% since the previous report, adequate crossings on operation trails increased by 17%.

This year's results are largely consistent with previous reports and continue to show that Maine's forestry and logging communities are using BMPs effectively. BMP use and effectiveness at timber harvesting operations are monitored regularly by the MFS District Foresters and Water Resources Specialist. In addition, MFS staff provide regular training and support for their application, with presentations and workshops across the state.

Since 2000, MFS staff have conducted a systematic statewide monitoring program of BMPs on a sample of timber harvesting operations across the state. Support from Maine landowners, loggers, and foresters has been critical to its implementation and effectiveness. MFS efforts also include financial incentives for loggers and foresters to acquire temporary bridges, which are among the most effective measures to install stream crossings with minimal impact.

In the latest report, and throughout the programs history, monitoring shows that when sedimentation was observed, it was most often due to inadequate BMP application. The risk of detrimental impacts also greatly increases if they are not applied or applied incorrectly. Previous reports and numerous national studies have also documented that BMPs help protect water resources when properly applied. The latest findings reinforce that continued monitoring, education, and training are key to sustaining the success of forestry BMPs and their environmental benefits.

The report can be found on the MFS Forest Policy and Management Division website.

Reasons for the proposed changes to the list include adding species based on new taxonomy and new evidence of natural occurrence in the United States or U.S. territories, removing species no longer known to occur within the United States or U.S. territories, and changing names to reflect currently accepted taxonomy and nomenclature. item.title: US Labor Department finds railroad illegally terminated employee who refused to work during severe weather — U.S. Department of Labor — News Releases
item.description: LITTLE ROCK, AR – A U.S. Department of Labor Occupational Safety and Health Administration whistleblower investigation has concluded that Union Pacific Railroad Co. violated the Federal Railroad Safety Act when it removed from service and later terminated a North Little Rock yardman who notified management of nearby lightning and federal safety standards. OSHA determined that the employee voiced concerns about nearby lightning, cited OSHA and NOAA lightening safety guidelines, initiated a safety stand-down, and refused to work until the storm passed. Within minutes of the stand-down, Union Pacific removed the employee from service and was later charged with insubordination. Union Pacific terminated his employment on May 30, 2024.On June 10, 2026, OSHA ordered Union Pacific to remove from the employee’s employment records any reference of the incident, and pay back wages, lost benefits, compensatory and punitive damages totaling at least $304,869, and attorney’s fees. Union Pacific filed objections to OSHA’s order and has requested a hearing before a U.S. Department of Labor Administrative Law Judge.OSHA’s Whistleblower Protection Program enforces 25 whistleblower statutes that protect employees from retaliation for reporting violations of workplace airline, anti-money laundering, commercial motor carrier, consumer product, criminal antitrust, environmental, financial reform, food safety, health insurance reform, maritime, motor vehicle safety, nuclear, pipeline, public transportation agency, railroad, safety and health, securities, and tax laws.Editor’s note: The U.S. Department of Labor does not release the names of employees involved in whistleblower complaints.

item.title: Maine State Archives offers expanded digital access with Open Access — Maine Secretary of State — Bureau of Corporations, Elections & Commissions News
item.description: AUGUSTA, MAINE – Secretary of State Shenna Bellows today announced the official launch of Open Access, the Maine State Archives (MSA) new online platform for publicly accessible, digitized and born-digital public records. The platform can be accessed at https://digitalarchives.maine.gov or from the Maine State Archives section of the Secretary of State website. Open Access is the public-facing side of a strategic effort to maintain a digital preservation system for records of Maine state government. The system ensures the long-term preservation and accessibility of state records that are archival or subject to long-term retention. “From the beginning, I have been committed to improving efficiency and modernizing our systems to benefit Mainers and streamline access,” said Secretary Bellows . “Open Access will provide improved government transparency in a user-friendly platform that will be continuously expanded as more and more collections are imaged.” Overall, MSA’s collections span five centuries from the 1639 royal land grant to Sir Ferdinand Gorges to the 2024 papers of the Lewiston Tragedy Commission. One section of the site is devoted to Maine history before statehood, highlighting important records such as Revolutionary War land grants and the Rolls and Rosters Book of Orders for the 8th Division of the Maine Militia. The records of Maine’s involvement in the Civil War are extensive. Open Access currently holds just over 100,000 imaged records so far. “With more than 8 miles of documents in the Archives care, there is a long way to go to digitize them all, but it’s a great start,” said Maine State Archivist Christian Cotz. “We’re excited to continue to add records to the platform and provide Mainers from students to researchers with even more to discover each time they visit the site.” ###

The platform can be accessed at https://digitalarchives.maine.gov or from the Maine State Archives section of the Secretary of State website. 

Open Access is the public-facing side of a strategic effort to maintain a digital preservation system for records of Maine state government. The system ensures the long-term preservation and accessibility of state records that are archival or subject to long-term retention. 

“From the beginning, I have been committed to improving efficiency and modernizing our systems to benefit Mainers and streamline access,” said Secretary Bellows. “Open Access will provide improved government transparency in a user-friendly platform that will be continuously expanded as more and more collections are imaged.”

Overall, MSA’s collections span five centuries from the 1639 royal land grant to Sir Ferdinand Gorges to the 2024 papers of the Lewiston Tragedy Commission. One section of the site is devoted to Maine history before statehood, highlighting important records such as Revolutionary War land grants and the Rolls and Rosters Book of Orders for the 8th Division of the Maine Militia. The records of Maine’s involvement in the Civil War are extensive. Open Access currently holds just over 100,000 imaged records so far. 

“With more than 8 miles of documents in the Archives care, there is a long way to go to digitize them all, but it’s a great start,” said Maine State Archivist Christian Cotz. “We’re excited to continue to add records to the platform and provide Mainers from students to researchers with even more to discover each time they visit the site.”

Maine Paid Family and Medical Leave Program Publishes Actuarial Report, First Claims Report

October 1, 2026

For Immediate Release: Oct. 1, 2026

Media Contact: Autumn Mahoney, Communications Specialist media.dol@maine.gov

Actuarial report projects PFML Trust Fund will remain stable for the next 10 years

AUGUSTA - The Maine Paid Family and Medical Leave (PFML) program has published its second annual actuarial report, as well as its first claims report on Oct. 1, 2026.

PFML became law in 2023 and is a statewide program that provides eligible workers with up to 12 weeks of paid leave for medical, parental, family care, military family or safe leave.

The PFML program began accepting claims on March 30, 2026, and began paying benefits on May 1, 2026. This initial claims report covers the program's first three months of claims activity, from March 30 through June 30, 2026. Future claims reports will be published annually and will cover a full year of claims activity.

Highlights of the reports include:

  • The PFML Trust Fund remains solvent and based on updated revenue and claim expenditure, is projected to remain stable for the next 10 years.
  • The program received 8,376 applications between March 30 and June 30, 2026.
  • Among the claims approved, medical leave was the most common reason, followed by welcoming a new child and caring for a family member. Other leave reasons represented a very small portion of the overall claim volume.

"We are excited to see the PFML Program effectively off the ground and helping Maine workers and businesses through life's big moments, both now and for years to come," said PFML Director Luke Monahan.

More information on the PFML program, including how to apply, can be found on the program's website: https://www.maine.gov/paidleave/

Employees, employers and self-employed individuals with questions can call 207-621-5024 between8 a.m. and 5 p.m. Monday through Friday. Employees can send a message through the Benefits Application Portal, while employers and self-employed individuals can send a message through the Maine Paid Leave Contributions Portal.

To Providers of Adult or Children's Services to Individuals with Intellectual Disabilities (ID) or Autism

Oct 02, 2026

The State of Maine Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) Office of Aging and Disability Services (OADS) is planning to launch the new Lifespan Waiver in May 2027. 

Our first priority is to offer support for future providers of Lifespan services.  Following our Lifespan Provider Readiness project in 2025, we are reaching out to understand provider interest in offering services under Lifespan. To that end, we created a survey to gauge interest from providers who serve individuals fourteen or older who have ID or autism. 

Please take a few minutes to complete this survey. 

The survey will be open until Friday, October 16, at 4:00 PM.  

Filling out the survey does not obligate an agency to provide services. We are both gauging interest in particular services, but also gathering contact information so we can provide technical assistance to agencies. For example, we hope to sustain Communities of Practice, and provide training opportunities. 

For questions, please contact the OADS Lifespan Project. 

Thank you for your interest, and we look forward to being in contact regarding Lifespan. 

~ The OADS Team

Hello, this is Governor Janet Mills, and thank you for listening.

Some years ago, there was a young woman who dated a man who was handsome and charming and smart, and she was in love with him. That man was also an alcoholic, as it turned out. And one night, in a drunken rage, he held a gun to her head.

The gun did not go off. She packed her bags and left that place and never turned back. Well, the rest of the story is that that young woman went to law school. She became a prosecutor, later Attorney General, and now the Governor of the State of Maine.

Yes, I was one of the lucky ones.

Many others who experienced domestic abuse are not so lucky. So to make sure that Maine people who have experienced or who are experiencing domestic abuse know that they're not alone and know that escape from violence is possible, I have declared October Domestic Violence Awareness Month in Maine. 

Here are some things you ought to know about domestic abuse and domestic violence. Domestic abuse and domestic violence affect people and families of all races, ages, genders, and income levels. Nationwide, one in four women and one in seven men has experienced abuse and violence by an intimate partner in their lifetime. In Maine, nearly half of all homicides are related to domestic abuse every year.

We can prevent domestic abuse and domestic violence in Maine by spreading awareness, by improving public policies to better support people affected by abuse, and by holding perpetrators accountable.

Every day, but especially during Domestic Violence Awareness Month, may we all do our part to spread awareness about domestic abuse, to challenge the behavior of abusive people, and to support survivors of abuse, whoever they may be. Together, our individual actions are what will end domestic abuse in the state of Maine.

So if you or someone you know is experiencing abuse, please call the statewide Domestic Abuse Helpline at 1-866-834-HELP. That's 1-866-834-HELP. If you or someone you know is deaf or hard of hearing, please call 1-800-437-1220. That's 1-800-437-1220.

item.title: Fisheries of the Northeastern United States; Summer Flounder Fishery; Quota Transfer From North Carolina to Massachusetts — Federal Register — Documents Matching 'Maine'
item.description: NMFS announces that the State of North Carolina is transferring a portion of its 2026 commercial summer flounder quota to the Commonwealth of Massachusetts. This adjustment to the 2026 fishing year quota is necessary to comply with the Summer Flounder, Scup, and Black Sea Bass Fishery Management Plan (FMP) quota transfer provisions. This announcement informs the public of the revised 2026 commercial quotas for North Carolina and Massachusetts.
